response.text:
I'll work through both draft chapters systematically, applying each test to sentences that could be structurally damaged.

---

**Ch 021 draft — checking sentence by sentence**

"That field of education seemed closed too." — The source ties this to the deaths of Mrs. Milnes Gaskell and Miss Charlotte Wynn (authorized removals) plus Milnes Gaskell leaving Parliament. The draft drops those names (authorized) but keeps the summarizing sentence "Death had ravaged one's circle of friends." A reader can follow: death ravaged the circle → that field closed. Borderline, but the logical chain is intact. Not a finding.

"He gladly set down Reeve's refusal of the Gold Conspiracy to respectability and editorial law, but when he sent the manuscript on to the Quarterly…" — The draft drops the entire "He gladly set down…to respectability and editorial law" sentence and jumps straight to "When he sent the manuscript on to the Quarterly, the editor of the Quarterly also refused it." The word "also" implies a prior refusal was *just explained/contextualized*, but in the draft the prior paragraph ended with the plain refusal and Reeve's libel-suit reason. The "also" still parses because Reeve's refusal was described immediately before. Not a broken pivot.

"As usual, when an ally was needed, the American was driven into the arms of the radicals. Respectability, everywhere and always, turned its back the moment one asked to do it a favor." — In the source, between the second Quarterly refusal and this sentence, there is: "Adams had no choice but to realize that he had to deal in 1870 with the same old English character of 1860, and the same inability in himself to understand it." The draft cuts that sentence. The "As usual" + "Respectability…turned its back" pivot reads as a conclusion following something — and the draft does have the double refusal just above, so the logical chain holds. Not a finding.

"Two long, dry, quarterly articles, appearing in quick succession, and pirated for audiences running well into the hundred thousands; and not one person…" — The source has "Here was a tour de force he had never dreamed himself equal to performing: two long…" The draft cuts "Here was a tour de force…equal to performing:" and leaves the fragment "Two long, dry, quarterly articles, appearing in quick succession…and not one person, man or woman, offering him so much as a congratulation." This is a sentence without a main verb — a nominal fragment. A reader hits it and has no predicate. This passes the non-parseable test.

"He sought education; he did not sell it." — In the source this sentence is embedded in a paragraph about Henry knowing Gurney, feeling influenced by his advice, and considering the professorship. The draft cuts the preceding context (Gurney, the double load, seeing no relation between himself and a professorship) and jumps to "He sought education; he did not sell it." The pronoun "he" has an antecedent (Adams) and the sentence parses on its own as a standalone aphorism. A reader can follow it. Not a finding.

---

**Ch 022 draft — checking sentence by sentence**

"The Pteraspis grins horribly from the closed entrance." — This sentence appears in the middle of the draft's discussion of historical method. In the source (Ch 022) it is preceded by "complexity precedes evolution." The draft keeps that. The sentence is retained from source. Pteraspis as a figure was introduced in the source's Ch 022 geological excursus — but that excursus is an *authorized removal* from Ch 017/021. However, the Pteraspis reference in Ch 022 source is *within Ch 022 itself*, not imported from the authorized cut chapters, and the draft *keeps* the sentence with its preceding clause "complexity precedes evolution. The Pteraspis grins horribly from the closed entrance." A reader unfamiliar with the geological subplot will find "Pteraspis" opaque, but it functions here as a metaphor for the closed-off beginning of history, which the immediately preceding clause ("complexity precedes evolution") contextualizes. The source does not gloss it differently in this passage. Not a finding — the missing gloss is a residue of the authorized Ch 017 digression removal.

"As a companion, King's charm was great, but King had moulded and directed his life logically, scientifically…" — Source: "As a companion, King's charm was great, but this was not the quality that so much attracted Adams, nor could he affect even distant rivalry on this ground. Adams could never tell a story…King and the Fortieth Parallel influenced him in a way far more vital. The lines of their lives converged, but King had moulded…" The draft cuts "this was not the quality that so much attracted Adams…King and the Fortieth Parallel influenced him in a way far more vital. The lines of their lives converged," and jumps straight to "but King had moulded and directed his life logically." The "but" is supposed to pivot from "King's charm was great [as a companion]" to something contrasting — in the source, the contrast is "but this was NOT what attracted Adams; what attracted him was King's directed life." The draft's version reads: "King's charm was great, but King had moulded his life logically" — which makes "charm" contrast with "moulded his life logically" as if these are opposites, which is not what is meant. The logical pivot is broken: the "but" now connects two positive attributes of King rather than pivoting to what actually drew Adams. A reader is genuinely misled about the argumentative structure.

"When the first year of professing and editing was at last over, he took the next train for the West." — The source has a substantial transition: Adams putting the July North American in his pocket with a notice of the Fortieth Parallel Survey, starting for the plains. The draft cuts the transition material (authorized: Western geological field-trip subplot). The sentence itself parses fine and no mid-scene jump issue since the West trip was authorized to be compressed. Not a finding.

"One morning when the party was camped high above Estes Park, on the flank of Long's Peak, he borrowed a rod, and rode down for some trout." — The source has: "Adams enjoyed killing big game…he liked to wander off alone on his mule, and pass the day fishing…One morning when the party was camped…he borrowed a rod, and rode down over a rough trail into Estes Park, for some trout." The draft cuts the setup about Adams's habits on the survey trip and jumps to the morning scene. The "he" refers clearly to Adams, established throughout. The authorized removal of the Western field-trip subplot covers this compression. Not a finding.

"Darkness caught him before he could catch his trail." — Source establishes the fishing day at length; draft omits it but this sentence still parses. Not a finding.
